**Video:** [Lec 10 — Challenge With ML](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=767MLwniPKE)

### Learning goals
- State the central challenge: $p$ is completely unknown; we only have samples
- Call a density estimate a **model**
- Learn the three-step recipe: choose $p_{\theta}$, choose a divergence, optimize $\theta$
- See why “all models are wrong; some are useful”

### Before this clicks
We want to estimate a density $p$ (joint / marginal / conditional — same mathematical job, different interpretation). A parametric family is a collection of densities indexed by parameters $\theta$.

---

## 1. Central problem (again)

$$
\mathcal{D}=\{x_i\}_{i=1}^{n}\ \text{i.i.d. from unknown density }p.
$$

(Writing “sample from a density” is slight abuse — sampling is from the distribution — but this is the course’s working language.)

Whether we write $p(x)$, $p(x,y)$, $p(y\mid x)$, … the **estimation task** is the same shape.

**Challenge:** we know **nothing** a priori about $p$. We are not totally blind only because we have **samples**.

---

## 2. What is a “model”?

Any algorithm’s estimate of the unknown density is called a **model**.

Large language models, classifiers, GMMs, … — in this worldview they are density (or conditional-density) estimators.

> All models are wrong; some are useful.  
> (All estimators are imperfect; usefulness is judged by a metric / task.)

There is no single correct density estimator; we compare them by how well they serve a chosen divergence / downstream goal.

---

## 3. Three-step recipe for density estimation

### Step 1 — Model choice: pick a parametric family

Assume

$$
p \approx p_{\theta}
$$

for some parameter $\theta$ in a family you choose.

Examples of families:

| Family | Typical $\theta$ |
|--------|------------------|
| Linear / logistic-style forms | weights $w$ |
| Gaussian $\mathcal{N}(\mu,\Sigma)$ | $(\mu,\Sigma)$ |
| Mixture models, kernels, neural nets, transformers | their internal parameters |

**Neural nets** are popular because they are **universal approximators**: with enough capacity they can approximate very broad classes of functions. Choosing the family is still a leap of faith: if truth is quadratic and you only allow lines, you are stuck with a bad model class. The optimizer will only find the **best line**, not invent a parabola.

Correction noted in a later lecture: for $w_1^{\top}x+w_2$, if $x\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ then $w_1\in\mathbb{R}^{D}$ and $w_2$ is a **scalar** (dimensions must match).

### Step 2 — Choose a “distance” between $p$ and $p_{\theta}$

Need a function

$$
d(p,p_{\theta})\ \ge\ 0
$$

measuring how far the model is from truth.

Quotes around “distance”: many ML divergences are **not** metrics (not symmetric, may fail triangle inequality). They are still useful. KL divergence (Lectures 11–12) is the star example in this course.

**Apparent paradox:** $d$ seems to need the unknown $p$. Later tools (likelihoods, empirical averages, LLN, …) let us optimize without writing $p$ explicitly.

### Step 3 — Train: optimize parameters

$$
\theta^{\star}
=\arg\min_{\theta}\, d\bigl(p,\,p_{\theta}\bigr).
$$

Finding $\theta^{\star}$ is what people call **training** the model.

Different algorithms = different $(p_{\theta},\ d,\ \text{optimizer})$ triples.

---

## 4. Why hundreds of algorithms?

If density estimation were one easy closed form, we would not need so many methods. The hardness is:

- unknown $p$,
- high-dimensional $x$,
- choice of family and divergence,
- computational optimization.

The rest of the course instantiates this recipe many times.

---

## 5. Tiny concrete example

Suppose scalar data and we choose the family of 1D Gaussians

$$
p_{\theta}(x)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi\sigma^{2}}}\exp\Bigl(-\frac{(x-\mu)^{2}}{2\sigma^{2}}\Bigr),\quad
\theta=(\mu,\sigma^{2}).
$$

Step 1 fixes “truth is somehow Gaussian.”  
Step 2 might use KL or equivalently maximize likelihood (later).  
Step 3 returns $(\hat\mu,\hat\sigma^{2})$ — e.g. sample mean and variance.

If the true density is a two-peak mixture, every Gaussian is wrong; some Gaussians are still “least bad” under your divergence.

---

## 6. Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|----------------|
| Training invents the model class | Training only fits $\theta$ inside the class you chose. |
| One correct model | Estimators are approximations; usefulness is relative. |
| Divergence must be a mathematical metric | KL & friends often are not; still OK. |
| $p(x)$ vs $p(y\mid x)$ are different problems | Same estimation template; different target density. |
